summary:
We build the Astronaut Health Monitor, a web app that helps astronauts assess their own health as well as their crew mates. Each day, a crew member completes a short check-in: heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen, body temp, sleep and mood, with instructions for taking each measurement. Instead of fixed limits, the app compares each reading to the astronauts 14 day average. Unusual readings are flagged as caution or alert.
Results appear on a clickable, color-coded body figure, with trend charts, and a crew overview. Each body system explains the related spaceflight hazard with links to its NASA source. Guidance with what to do is included.
This is important because on a mission on Mars or any other far planet, it would take Earth minutes to get any messages. The assessment is entirely on board, giving crews, fast, personal decision support when help is far away. Right now, data is simulated.
details:
What it does and how it works

The Astronaut Health Monitor is a web app that guides astronauts through a daily health check and tells them what to do next. It follows a four-step loop:

  1. Measure: a guided check-in for seven indicators: heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, blood oxygen (SpO2), body temperature, sleep duration and mood. Each one has "how to take this measurement" instructions, and impossible values, for example oxygen 100% are rejected.
  2. Assess: the backend compares each new reading to that astronaut's own baseline, the average and normal variation of their last 14 days. More than 2 standard deviations away is Caution, and more than 3 is Alert. With fewer than 5 readings, the app says it is still building a baseline.
  3. Understand: results appear on a clickable, color-coded body figure (heart, lungs, sleep, mood and body temperature). Clicking a body part shows the latest values, the person's average values, why that system matters in spaceflight, the related hazard, and links to NASA sources. A trend chart shows each indicator over time against a dashed "your average" line, and a crew overview compares every crew member side by side.(note: the brain is there and was considered for cognitive testing but we were not able to get to that)
  4. Act: tiered guidance: self-care, tell the crew medical officer, or contact flight surgeons based off of urgency.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Autonomy: the assessment runs on board, with no connection to Earth needed. That matters when messages take minutes each way.
  • Personal, not generic: spaceflight changes the body (for example, astronauts can run warmer than on Earth), so comparing people to their own normal avoids false alarms and catches changes that fixed limits would miss.
  • Fast and clear: one screen shows what's wrong, why it matters, and who to involve.
  • Crew-wide awareness: the crew medical officer can check everyone at a glance.

Our intended impact is giving crews quick, trustworthy decision support so small changes are caught before they become serious. The same approach could also help people in remote places on Earth, such as research stations.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Recharts (charts), hand-built SVG body figure, custom CSS theme
  • Backend: Java 21, Spring Boot (Spring Web, Spring Data JPA, Validation), H2 database, Maven, JUnit tests
  • Workflow: Git and GitHub (branches and pull requests), a shared API contract, VS Code and IntelliJ
  • Design: Canva (logo and slides), SVG Repo icons, Instrument Serif and Newsreader fonts
  • AI assistance: Claude as a coding assistant (documented in our README)
  • Hardware: N/A

What makes it creative

  • Personal baselines instead of fixed thresholds: each astronaut is their own reference point.
  • A body figure that explains itself: every body part links to its spaceflight hazard and NASA source, turning a status color into understanding.
  • "Your average" on every chart: you can see at a glance when a reading is unusual for that person.
  • Built for disconnection: designed around the "distance from Earth" hazard.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: NASA doesn't publish simple fixed ranges for these indicators, so we didn't invent any. Every explanation cites a NASA or space-agency source.
  • Safety: the app is decision support, never a diagnosis, and it always points to a person to involve.
  • Transparency: all demo data is simulated and labeled, and AI use is documented in the README.
  • Accessibility: status is shown with both color and text.
  • Honest scope: we cover cardiovascular, respiratory, temperature, sleep and behavioral health. Radiation, bone loss and immune changes are next steps, along with wearable sensors and multi-day trend alerts.
